extracted.intended_audience: university educators, tutors, and students (especially in Catholic universities)
extracted.subtask_short: teaching Latin and religion at university
extracted.subtask_description: Prescriptive guidance on methods and curriculum for University instruction in Latin composition and general religious knowledge, aimed at shaping what to teach, how to teach it, and what students should know. Emphasises inductive/imitative methods for Latin and a defined, examinable place for religion in a secular faculty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good Latinity lies in structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Good Latinity lies in structure; every word of a sentence may be Latin, yet the whole sentence remain English; dictionaries do not teach composition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Learn Latinity by analyzing models (Cicero) to see what is possible in Latin composition: force of words, combination into phrases, collocation, carrying on of subject/nominative through a sentence, breaking a sentence into clauses, evasion of categorical form, resolution of abstract nouns into verbs and participles. Use examples to form principles; compensate for want of brevity by elegance; secure perspicuity by figures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Learn Latin by induction and imitation (not by rules alone)
rubrics_metrics.description: Rules and remarks in composition-books do not by themselves produce the idea of Latinity; one must make an induction from exemplary writers rather than rely on abstract rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Turn Cicero (and similar masters) into raw materials for induction: keep blank books noting every peculiarity, analyze phrase and sentence structure, form one's own rules from observed patterns. Use books as patterns to copy and as capital to improve; be active — 'self-taught, yet without oddities, and tutorized, yet without conventionalities.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Include Religion in the School of Arts on an intelligible principle
rubrics_metrics.description: If religious instruction has a place in a secular Faculty it should be determined on some intelligible principle that justifies its introduction while preventing intrusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fix the conditions under which Religion is admitted so it is not a mere intrusion; justify inclusion on pragmatic and moral grounds (propriety, public opinion, inconvenience of neglect) and then decide content and scope accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat Religion as a branch of knowledge in the secular course
rubrics_metrics.description: Religion should be taught in the School of Philosophy and Letters simply as a branch of knowledge: sacred history alongside profane history, Biblical literature alongside ancient literature, and divine philosophy alongside human philosophy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frame religious subjects as part of general intellectual training (history, literature, philosophy). This legitimises teaching Biblical and ecclesiastical topics within a secular curriculum so long as they are treated in their historical/literary/philosophical aspects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Religious teaching must be examinable to secure student attention
rubrics_metrics.description: If the subject of Religion is to have a real place in their course of study, it must enter into the examinations in which that course results; nothing will impress and occupy their minds but what they must present to Examiners.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include religious topics in formal assessment to ensure students prepare and take the subject seriously; examinations define and stabilise the scope of teaching in practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit doctrinal theology in secular schools; enforce broad catechetical knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: Exclude teaching in extenso of pure dogma from the secular schools; content should be limited to a broad knowledge of doctrinal subjects as found in the catechisms of the Church or in writings suitable to the laity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage study of religion in its secular/applicable aspects (history, literature, philosophy, evidences, 'Notes of the Church'), but avoid in-depth systematic dogmatic instruction in secular lecture-rooms which may be inappropriate for lay or secular faculties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expected scope of students' religious knowledge (practical/lay level)
rubrics_metrics.description: Students should acquire general facts and an intelligent apprehension of Christianity and Church history suitable for social intercourse and public life—e.g., primitive divisions of Christianity, polity, luminaries, great eras, propagation history, list of Fathers, names and roles of notable figures, the canon of Scripture, languages of Scripture, contents and authors of biblical books.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for practical, usable knowledge rather than exhaustive specialization: be able to answer common civic or conversational questions (difference between Church and sect, canon history, who key Fathers were, what the Church has done for learning). Superficial knowledge in these historical and factual areas is acceptable and often desirable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Encourage supervised reading of apologetic and polemical works (external/Philosophy of Religion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Lay students may read works of the external contemplation of Religion (Philosophy of Religion) and selected apologetic/polemical writings by lay and ecclesiastical authors; such reading is suitable provided it is the external/philosophical treatment rather than in-depth dogmatics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recommended reading can include Origen’s work against Celsus, Tertullian’s Apology, Augustine’s City of God, selections from Bellarmine, Suarez on laws, and other controversial treatises; exercise discretion and confine treatment to philosophical/polemical aspects. Supervision and explanation by experienced teachers are implied.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supervise students' religious reading and study
rubrics_metrics.description: Whatever students read in the province of Religion, they should read under the superintendence and with the explanations of those older and more experienced than themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure tutors or senior scholars guide and contextualize students' readings to prevent superficial misunderstanding or misapplication; supervision mitigates risks of error from partial learning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer open, candid engagement with unbelief
rubrics_metrics.description: An age in which unbelief speaks out is preferable to one in which unbelief masquerades as faith; open confrontation allows Truth to speak out and entrench itself clearly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage frank debate and toleration: when unbelief is avowed it permits clearer definition, confident institutional defence, and the ability for a University to display and define its professed beliefs unequivocally.
